titulo.texto: Great Mural and Ethnolinguistic Map of Mexico

frase_gancho.texto: A map where the languages of Mexico are still alive.

puente_narrativo.texto: We move from words to the places where they are spoken. Look for a house with walls of sticks and mud, a thatched roof, and a hearth with three stones in the center.

guion_corto.texto: This great map shows where the Indigenous peoples of Mexico live today and which language each one speaks. In all, there are sixty-eight peoples, with their languages, grouped into eleven language families. More than seven million people speak an Indigenous language. Notice how they are spread across the territory: there are languages of the desert, the mountains, the jungle, and the coast, and the south, above all Oaxaca, is full of colors. The ethnographic cartography of this hall, begun by the painter Luis Covarrubias for the 1964 inauguration and now accompanied by updated audiovisual displays, shows that vitality. Here there is not just one Mexico: there are many, and all of them are spoken.

guion_largo.texto:
On the ground floor, almost everything you saw was in the past tense. Here you go upstairs, and the museum changes its verb tense. The halls upstairs were put together in the 1960s, after expeditions throughout the country to get to know the Indigenous peoples, collect their objects and, in some cases, invite their own communities to build their houses inside the museum. The idea was to show the people of today, not a postcard past.

And the people of today talk a lot. Sixty-eight peoples, with sixty-eight languages, grouped into eleven language families and more than three hundred sixty variants. These are not dialects of a single language: they are languages as different from one another as Spanish and Hungarian, which are not related. Nahuatl and Maya, for example, come from families that do not resemble each other at all. It is one of the greatest diversities of languages in the Americas.

Look on the map for the peoples you already know. The Nahua, descendants of the Mexica, form the largest group. The Maya remain in the Yucatán Peninsula and in Chiapas, and their languages total more than two million speakers. The Zapotec and Mixtec live in Oaxaca, where you saw Monte Albán. The Purépecha, in Michoacán. And the Huastec, who speak a language of the Maya branch, called Teenek, remain on the Gulf Coast, far from their relatives in the south.

Many words you use every day come from these languages. Chocolate, tomato, avocado, coyote, and chalk are Nahuatl words. The Spanish slang word “cuate,” which we use to say “friend,” comes from a Nahuatl word that means “twin.” And the word “Mexico” is also Nahuatl; according to a widely held explanation, it means “in the navel of the moon,” although specialists still debate its exact origin.

Not everything is cause for celebration: many languages have fewer and fewer speakers, because over generations people were taught that speaking them was an obstacle. Some are on the verge of disappearing. Today many communities teach them in schools and use them on the radio and on social media. The United Nations declared the period from twenty twenty-two to twenty thirty-two the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.

Another fact to consider calmly. The map was painted in the 1960s, and it has been updated, but any map of languages falls short: people move, migrate to cities, travel. There are Mixtec speakers in Mexico City and Zapotec speakers in California. Languages no longer stay where they began.

That is why this map is not a museum piece in the sense of those downstairs. It changes, just like the people who live in it. In the next halls you will see how each people, with its language, its food, its clothing, and its festivals, builds its own way of being Mexican. How many of these languages have you ever heard spoken?

texto.Indigenous People: Plurinational (68 ethnolinguistic groups and 11 language families)
texto.Historical authorship and museography: Original cartography by Luis Covarrubias (1964) and updated interactive infographic (INAH/INALI)

texto.pregunta: Myth: Indigenous languages are simply dialects of a single language.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They are distinct languages, from families that are not related to one another. In Mexico, sixty-eight Indigenous languages are spoken, with more than three hundred variants.
